domain: Anesthesia monitoring & equipment (anesthesia machine & circuits, ventilators, capnography & gas analysis, pulse oximetry, depth of anesthesia, neuromuscular monitoring, alarms & safety checks)
stem: What is the most common risk factor for a surgical fire in the operating room?
answer: Open delivery of oxygen (the most common surgical fire risk factor)
rationale: Oxygen enriches the environment making ignition far easier; open delivery near an ignition source is the classic setup for OR fire.
confusable_with: Electrocautery alone (ignition source but not the primary risk factor without oxidizer)

domain: Anesthesia monitoring & equipment (anesthesia machine & circuits, ventilators, capnography & gas analysis, pulse oximetry, depth of anesthesia, neuromuscular monitoring, alarms & safety checks)
stem: In what surgical scenario is surgical fire most commonly reported?
answer: Supplemental oxygen delivery with surgical site above the xiphoid (head, neck, or upper chest procedures)
rationale: Oxygen accumulates under drapes near the face/airway, and electrocautery or laser provides the ignition source in a confined space.
confusable_with: Abdominal surgery (below xiphoid, lower risk)

domain: Anesthesia monitoring & equipment (anesthesia machine & circuits, ventilators, capnography & gas analysis, pulse oximetry, depth of anesthesia, neuromuscular monitoring, alarms & safety checks)
stem: What oxygen concentration threshold guides safe administration during procedures with open oxygen delivery near the surgical field?
answer: Concentrations greater than 30% oxygen should be guided by clinical need and avoided when possible with open delivery above the xiphoid
rationale: Oxygen enrichment above 30% dramatically increases combustibility of drapes, hair, and airway secretions near the surgical field.
confusable_with: 100% FiO2 is always safe (incorrect; high FiO2 elevates fire risk significantly)

domain: Anesthesia monitoring & equipment (anesthesia machine & circuits, ventilators, capnography & gas analysis, pulse oximetry, depth of anesthesia, neuromuscular monitoring, alarms & safety checks)
stem: Should conventional endotracheal tubes be wrapped with metallic foil to reduce laser ignition risk?
answer: Wrapping conventional ETTs with foil should be avoided; laser-specific tubes are required instead
rationale: Conventional foil wrapping provides inconsistent protection and the sharp foil edges can damage tissue; dedicated laser-resistant tubes are designed for this purpose.
confusable_with: Foil-wrapping as an acceptable laser precaution

domain: Anesthesia monitoring & equipment (anesthesia machine & circuits, ventilators, capnography & gas analysis, pulse oximetry, depth of anesthesia, neuromuscular monitoring, alarms & safety checks)
stem: What fire prevention principle is emphasized by the Anesthesia Patient Safety Foundation for OR fires?
answer: Heavy emphasis on risks of open delivery of oxygen; educational video and online modules developed by APSF
rationale: Education and behavioral change around oxygen delivery practices are the most effective primary prevention strategies for OR fires.
confusable_with: Focusing only on ignition sources (drapes, laser) without addressing the oxidizer

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: Excessive fluid administration in the perioperative period impairs what physiological processes?
answer: Impairs oxygen transport, tissue healing, bowel function return; increases risk of surgical site infection
rationale: Tissue edema from fluid overload reduces diffusion distance for oxygen, compromises gut motility, and creates a pro-infective tissue milieu.
confusable_with: Underresuscitation causing the same harms (both extremes are harmful)

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: In large-volume crystalloid administration, what metabolic acid-base disturbance can normal saline cause?
answer: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis from large-volume normal saline
rationale: NS has a chloride concentration of 154 mEq/L; large volumes cause chloride loading which reduces renal bicarbonate reabsorption producing non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
confusable_with: Lactic acidosis (different etiology)

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: When hemodynamic monitoring is used to guide AKI prevention, what parameter is targeted per KDIGO guidelines?
answer: Mean arterial pressure and volume status; adequate hemodynamic support to maintain renal perfusion pressure
rationale: KDIGO recommendations emphasize maintaining adequate MAP and euvolemia to prevent renal hypoperfusion-mediated AKI.
confusable_with: Targeting CVP as the sole fluid adequacy marker (now disfavored)

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: What balanced crystalloid is preferred over normal saline in brain injury or when diluting packed red blood cells?
answer: Normal saline is preferred in brain injury and for diluting pRBCs; balanced crystalloids (LR, Plasma-Lyte) preferred otherwise
rationale: Hypotonicity risk with hypotonic solutions in cerebral edema and compatibility with pRBC transfusion favors NS in specific contexts.
confusable_with: LR for all situations including brain injury (incorrect due to slight hypotonicity)

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: Ultrasonography of the inferior vena cava in acute blood loss can reveal what sign of severe hypovolemia?
answer: Nearly collapsed or incompletely filled IVC on ultrasonography indicates severe hypovolemia
rationale: IVC collapsibility with respiration reflects low right atrial filling pressure and intravascular volume depletion.
confusable_with: Plethoric non-collapsing IVC (indicates fluid overload or elevated RAP)

domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal physiology, congenital heart, pediatric airway, fluid/glucose management, regional in children)
stem: Using the Holliday-Segar formula, what is the maintenance fluid rate for a 25 kg child?
answer: First 10 kg: 40 mL/h; next 10 kg: +20 mL/h (2 mL/kg/h); next 5 kg: +5 mL/h (1 mL/kg/h) = 65 mL/h total
rationale: The 4-2-1 rule provides weight-based maintenance rates that match insensible and renal losses in children.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Hemorrhagic Shock Classification & Management

confusable_with: Adult weight-based dosing applied directly to children

domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal physiology, congenital heart, pediatric airway, fluid/glucose management, regional in children)
stem: In neonates with abdominal wall defects, what two fluid management principles apply?
answer: Attention to fluid replacement and temperature management (both are critical in NEC and abdominal wall defect surgery)
rationale: Exposed bowel causes large evaporative and third-space fluid losses and dramatic heat loss, requiring aggressive replacement.
confusable_with: Standard adult perioperative fluid protocols

domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal physiology, congenital heart, pediatric airway, fluid/glucose management, regional in children)
stem: In a premature infant with respiratory distress syndrome, what complication of wide swings in oxygen tension can affect retinal vessels?
answer: Retinopathy of prematurity from oxygen tension fluctuations in premature ventilated infants with RDS
rationale: Hyperoxia followed by hypoxia drives VEGF-mediated abnormal retinal neovascularization in immature vessels.
confusable_with: Retinal artery occlusion (arterial, not proliferative)

domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal physiology, congenital heart, pediatric airway, fluid/glucose management, regional in children)
stem: What is the maximum safe peripheral IV replacement rate for potassium in pediatric patients?
answer: Peripheral IV potassium replacement should not exceed 8 mEq/h due to irritative effect on peripheral veins
rationale: Higher rates cause pain, phlebitis, and risk of inadvertent hyperkalaemia; central access is needed for faster replacement.
confusable_with: No rate limit via peripheral IV (incorrect; can cause vein sclerosis and cardiac dysrhythmia)

domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal physiology, congenital heart, pediatric airway, fluid/glucose management, regional in children)
stem: Why is awake endotracheal intubation virtually impossible in most pediatric patients with a difficult airway?
answer: Lack of patient cooperation in most pediatric age groups makes awake endotracheal intubation virtually impossible
rationale: Children cannot reliably cooperate with topical anaesthesia protocols, necessitating modified inhalational or intravenous induction strategies.
confusable_with: Awake fiberoptic intubation (feasible in cooperative adults, not typical pediatric patients)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: Aspiration or swallowing of a button battery presents what specific urgent risk?
answer: Rapid and severe tissue burns from increased battery current/voltage, causing tissue necrosis requiring emergency removal
rationale: Button batteries generate electrical current in moist tissue producing hydroxide radicals, causing liquefaction necrosis within hours.
confusable_with: Coin ingestion (usually can wait for elective removal)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: Even after initial surgical tracheostomy to secure an airway with laryngeal pathology, what intraoperative airway risk persists?
answer: Intraoperative airway obstruction from surgical manipulation, foreign body, or hemorrhage can occur even after tracheostomy
rationale: Tracheostomy secures the airway at rest but does not prevent dynamic obstruction from surgical complications during the procedure.
confusable_with: Tracheostomy guaranteeing a secure airway throughout surgery

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: What causes of upper airway obstruction must be evaluated before assuming a foreign body is the etiology?
answer: Papillomas, tracheal stenosis, tumors, vocal cord dysfunction must be excluded by preoperative history and physical examination
rationale: Multiple pathologies mimic foreign body obstruction; definitive diagnosis guides the safest airway management strategy.
confusable_with: Assuming all upper airway obstruction is a foreign body

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: What jaw-thrust maneuver step is described for opening the airway in an unconscious patient with possible foreign body obstruction?
answer: Stand at both sides of the head, grasp the angles of the jaw, and lift to open the airway
rationale: Jaw thrust opens the airway without neck extension and is the recommended maneuver in suspected cervical injury or unconscious patient.
confusable_with: Head-tilt chin-lift (contraindicated with potential cervical injury)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: Foreign body obstruction is listed under what category of causes of hypoxemia in the ICU setting?
answer: Foreign body is an upper airway cause of hypoxemia (under airway obstruction category in ICU differential)
rationale: Foreign body obstruction causes ventilatory failure by physical blockage of gas flow, distinct from V/Q mismatch or shunt etiologies.
confusable_with: Pulmonary embolism (vascular obstruction, not airway)
